title: Paramelaconite-Enriched Copper-Based Material as an Efficient and Robust Catalyst for Electrochemical Carbon Dioxide Reduction
abstract: Today and in the past, both the energy and chemistry sector have relied on fossil carbon resources as their primary fuel and carbon-based feedstock. At the beginning of the 20th century this was coal, later followed by oil and now moving toward shale gas. In the future, however, electrons obtained from renewable sources will take on the role of being the main energy feedstock. This will open new routes for the chemical industry, giving it the opportunity to make a radical shift and start producing useful molecules without having to burn part of their carbon feedstock for electricity or heating. As the simplest olefin, ethylene (C2H4) is one of the most significant building blocks for the chemical industry, with an annual production of 180 million tons in 2017 and its global market size reaching over 170 billion USD per year.[1] Ethylene is used for the production of most common plastics, such as polyethylene (packaging, cookware, toys), polyvinyl chloride (tubing, foils), polyethylene terephthalate (bottles, clothing) or via ethylene oxide in polyols (polyurethanes, foam, insulation). Currently, ethylene is produced by steam cracking of naphtha or thermal dehydrogenation of ethane from shale gas, which are energy demanding processes that take place at high temperatures (>1000K). These processes leave a considerable carbon footprint, emitting 1.4 tons of CO2 for every ton of ethylene produced.[1] In an effort to establish a green approach to ethylene production based on renewable energy, companies and academia have focused on exploring the electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR). This reaction represents a single step electrochemical synthesis of ethylene from CO2 and H2O (2 CO2 + 2 H2O → C2H4 + 3 O2). The energy needed for this process is supplied from carbon-neutral renewable energy sources such as wind and solar. Additionally, CO2 that is utilized as a feedstock can be captured at different point sources (fossil fuel power plants, cement factories, iron and steel industry, breweries, etc., and finally air). In Germany alone, emission of CO2 on a yearly level reaches ≈800 million tons, which would A copper-oxide-based catalyst enriched with paramelaconite (Cu4O3) is presented and investigated as an electrocatalyst for facilitating electroreduction of CO2 to ethylene and other hydrocarbons. Cu4O3 is a member of the copper-oxide family and possesses an intriguing mixedvalance nature, incorporating an equal number of Cu+ and Cu2+ ions in its crystal structure. The material is synthesized using a solvothermal synthesis route and its structure is confirmed via powder X-ray diffraction, transmission electron microscope based selected area electron diffraction, and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy. A flow reactor equipped with a gas diffusion electrode is utilized to test a copper-based catalyst enriched with the Cu4O3 phase under CO2 reduction conditions. The Cu4O3-rich catalyst (PrC) shows a Faradaic efficiency for ethylene over 40% at 400 mA cm−2. At −0.64 versus reversible hydrogen electrode, the highest C2+/C1 product ratio of 4.8 is achieved, with C2+ Faradaic efficiency over 61%. Additionally, the catalyst exhibits a stable performance for 24 h at a constant current density of 200 mA cm−2.

referenceMentions.context: Besides lowering the energy barrier for CC bond formation, the mixedvalence Cu4O3 surface possesses the ability to electrostatically stabilize the highly polar (OC)δ+(CO)δ-dimer that is proposed as an important intermediate in the formation of many C2+ products.[51] To date, there have been no experimental studies which investigated the catalytic activity of the paramelaconite phase for CO2RR.

sections.text:
Adv. Energy Mater. 2019, 1901228

be enough to supply the world demand for ethylene.[2] A wellknown challenge of renewable energy sources is their intermittent nature and production peaks that do not align with peaks in consumption. For example, in 2016 there was 3.7 TWh of stranded energy from renewable sources in Germany. Here too, the electrochemical CO2RR could play a vital role by turning this unused electricity into more than 265 thousand tons of ethylene.[2] This, however, amounts to only 0.15% of the global ethylene demand implying that scaling of renewable energy capacities will be needed to enable electrochemical feedstock production and to move away from traditional petrochemistry. Besides ethylene, other hydrocarbon CO2RR products such as ethanol, n-propanol and acetate are also highly desired for use as chemical feedstock and liquid fuels with high energy density. However, a key prerequisite to enable this bright, low-carbonfootprint future for electrochemical hydrocarbon production will be the development of a highly selective, efficient and durable electro-catalyst.
Among all transition metals, copper is the only catalyst capable of converting CO2 directly to a variety of hydrocarbons and oxygenates.[3] Using bulk copper catalysts comes with several limitations, such as poor selectivity toward specific valuable hydrocarbon products, high overpotentials, low activity due to limited surface area, and Faradaic efficiency (FE) losses caused by the competing hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). To overcome these problems, researchers have conducted numerous studies, which demonstrated that the catalytic performance of the copper catalysts for CO2RR can be greatly influenced by several different parameters. For example, Reller et al. designed a copper-based catalyst with a dendritic structure. The catalyst contains high number of high-index facets and under-coordinated sites which enabled high ethylene selectivity (FEC2H4 of 57%).
[4] These findings have been confirmed by other investigations where surface reconstruction[5,6] and morphology modification[4,7,8] have been shown to enhance activity and/or selectivity of copper-based catalysts compared to their bulk equivalents. The reason for their improved catalytic performance is usually linked to the increase in the density of low-coordinated active sites (e.g., edge sites) that exhibit an enhanced CO adsorption and reduce the energy barrier for CC coupling,[9,10] thus favoring formation of long-chain
products. Currently, oxide-derived copper (OD-Cu) catalysts are in the spotlight due to their high ethylene selectivity and CO2RR activity, which has been attributed to the formation of numerous grain boundaries during oxidative/reductive treatment, increased surface roughness, oxidation state of the surface layer, residual bulk oxides and subsurface oxygen.[11–15] Although it has been suggested that presence of Cu+ surface species during CO2RR plays an important role in achieving high ethylene selectivity,[7,16,17] recent experimental[18,19] and theoretical work[20,21] has pointed out that these surface species are unstable under the reducing potentials that occur during cell operation. Even though it is unlikely that Cu+ and Cu2+ surface species are present during CO2RR, looking back on the previous work done on copper-oxide-based catalysts, it is clear that the initial oxidation state of the catalyst’s surface has an effect on the CO2RR product distribution.[22–24] The initial copper oxides most probably act as precatalyst for the formation of suitable Cu surface facets by in-situ reduction during CO2RR.
Together with high activity and selectivity, another crucial parameter for the commercialization of CO2RR technology is the stability of the developed catalysts. Although, the current state-of-the-art copper-based catalysts are able to achieve high FEs for hydrocarbon products, maintaining a stable, long-term selectivity for these products at industrially relevant current densities (>200 mA cm−2) has been recognized as problematic. During our studies on copper-based catalysts for CO2RR, we realized that certain copper powders show increased selectivity for ethylene and a more stable performance. We employed powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) to investigate the mentioned powders and discovered that all of them contain traces of “impurity” which we later identified as the rather unknown paramelaconite (Cu4O3) phase. Based on these preliminary findings, we have developed a copper-oxide-based material enriched with paramelaconite. Together with cuprous oxide (Cu2O) and cupric oxide (CuO), Cu4O3 is a member of the copper-oxide family and it is sometimes formally written as Cu+2Cu2+2O3.[25] Paramelaconite incorporates an equal number of monovalent and divalent copper ions in its tetragonal crystal structure (I41/amd), which consists of inter-penetrating Cu+-O and Cu2+-O chains, where Cu+ ions are two-fold coordinated, like in Cu2O, and Cu2+ ions are four-fold coordinated, like in
Adv. Energy Mater. 2019, 1901228
© 2019 WILEY-VCH Verlag GmbH & Co. KGaA, Weinheim1901228 (3 of 10)
CuO (Figure 1a).[26,27] Unlike Cu2O and CuO, paramelaconite has to-date never been tested as a catalyst for CO2RR. Recent theoretical work has suggested that copper catalysts with a mixture of Cu0 and Cu+ species on their initial surface improve the kinetics and thermodynamics of both CO2 activation and CC coupling compared to copper catalysts with a monovalent surface.[28] Based on the mentioned work, our intention was to take advantage of paramelaconite’s mixed-valence (Cu+ and Cu2+) nature to provide initial template surface active sites with multiple valences that would possibly enable high selectivity for hydrocarbon products and improved stability. Unlike the previously reported OD-Cu catalysts, which predominantly use Cu2O as a precursor for obtaining a reduced copper metallic active surface for CO2RR, we present here a catalyst on which active surface sites would be, in part, formed from reduced Cu4O3 during operation conditions.
Herein we demonstrate the suitability of a copper-oxidebased material enriched with paramelaconite as a catalyst for CO2RR. Copper-based catalyst powder enriched with spherical, micrometer-sized Cu4O3 particles was obtained using a scalable solvothermal synthesis route. The presence of paramelaconite in the synthesized powder was confirmed via PXRD, transmission electron microscope (TEM)-based selected area electron diffraction (SAED) and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). The Cu4O3-rich catalyst (PrC) was integrated into gas diffusion electrodes (GDEs), to overcome the transport limitations of CO2 supply in condensed media and therefore allow experiments at high current densities.[29] When tested for CO2RR, PrC exhibited a shift of selectivity from C1 to C2+ products with increasing negative potentials, reaching an FE maximum of 63% for C2+ products at −0.64 V versus RHE (jtot = 300 mA cm−2). The major CO2RR product was found to be ethylene with an FE of 43%. Besides high catalytic activity and selectivity, the PrC additionally showed an unprecedented long-term stable performance for 24 h, despite the high applied current density of 200 mA cm−2.

sections.heading: 2.1. Synthesis and Characterization of the Pristine Catalyst Material
sections.text:
We synthesized a copper-oxide-based catalyst powder enriched with paramelaconite using a modified and upscaled solvothermal synthesis method based on reacting copper (II) nitrate trihydrate (Cu(NO3)2·H2O) in the presence of N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF) and ethanol.[30] To induce the formation of the paramelaconite phase, addition of equimolar amounts of formic acid and dimethylamine to the reaction mixture was needed (additional and more detailed information regarding the synthesis route can be found in the Supporting Information). A PXRD pattern of the catalyst powder investigated in this study is shown in Figure 1b. The PXRD pattern shows that the synthesized catalyst consists predominantly of Cu4O3 and Cu2O phases, with traces of metallic Cu. Using the Rietveld method, we performed a quantitative phase analysis of the synthesized powder that estimated the phase compositions of the powder to be: 39 wt% of Cu4O3, 60 wt% of Cu2O, and 1 wt% of Cu.
The synthesis route was performed several times with good reproducibility. Catalyst powder was additionally characterized by scanning electron microscope (SEM) to investigate the morphology of synthesized particles. SEM images revealed the presence of smaller cubic-shaped particles and larger spherical particles (Figure 1b). It was found that the synthesis conditions strongly affect the phase compositions of the catalyst powders, as well as the shape and surface morphology of the particles. For example, the content of Cu4O3 present inside the catalyst powders could be influenced by manipulating the reaction time, as confirmed using PXRD (Figures S2 and S3, Supporting Information). Additionally, depending on the concentration of added formic acid and dimethylamine, the morphology of the synthesized particles was changed (Figure S4, Supporting Information). However, using this synthesis approach a fully paramelaconite phase-pure materials was not obtained.
Two distinct particle morphologies observed in the SEM image are in line with the data obtained from PXRD, which showed that the material is a mixture of primarily two phases, Cu4O3 and Cu2O. To better understand which copper-oxide phase corresponds to which particle morphology, we performed TEM-based SAED measurements on the powder to determine the phase composition of individual particles. A thin lamella for TEM characterization containing both, small cubic particles and large spherical-like particles, was prepared using a focused ion beam (FIB) (Figure 2a). By comparing the simulated SAED patterns (green spots in Figure 2d) to the experimental patterns, it was possible to identify the large spherical particles as paramelaconite and the smaller, cubic particles as copper (I) oxide. The elongated spots or arcs in the diffraction patterns indicate that each powder particle contains nanocrystalline grains that are textured about a direction at an angle to the beam. This preferred growth direction is expected based on current theories of how particles form during solvothermal synthesis.[31] Elemental maps (Figure 2b) of the particles were obtained by scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) in combination with energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX). Comparing the spectra from Cu4O3 and Cu2O particles, a difference in Cu K signal intensity is observed. A stronger Cu K signal intensity originating from the small cubic particles compared to large spherical particles supports the SAED results, which identified the cubes as Cu2O. During fabrication of the TEM lamella, the cross-section of the particles was additionally imaged using field-emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM). The obtained images (Figure 2c) reveal an inner porous structure of paramelaconite and copper (I) oxide. While Cu4O3 particles possess a relatively porous inner structure with a significant amount of open pores, Cu2O particles possess a denser inner structure with closed pores.
As both SAED and PXRD are bulk sensitive techniques, the surface chemical composition was assessed by ex situ XPS to investigate the catalytically relevant surface composition of the powder. The Cu 2p3/2 spectral region of the synthesized catalyst powder (PrC, red curve) is shown in Figure 3a, and compared to three standard samples, namely metallic Cu0 (yellow curve), Cu2O (blue curve), and CuO (green curve). The synthesized catalyst powder shows the presence of a shake-up satellite feature at ≈940–945 eV binding energy which is characteristic for d9 Cu2+ species that are typically not present in spectra of d10 Cu0

or Cu+ alone (see inset in Figure 3a).[32] On the other hand, the binding energy of the PrC’s main Cu 2p3/2 peak suggests the existence of Cu+ surface species. This can be concluded from the positions of the Cu 2p3/2 peak, whose binding energy of 932.4 eV is in good accordance with the Cu2O standard sample and literature values for Cu2O.[32] However, Cu+ species, like the ones in Cu2O, cannot be meaningfully distinguished from metallic Cu0 based solely on the Cu 2p3/2 peak binding energy. To shed further light on the chemical surface composition, Cu LMM Auger line spectra were additionally analyzed. The results are shown in Figure 3b. The PrC’s Cu L3M4,5M4,5 peak at 916.6 eV is in accordance with reported literature values and it also identifies well with the Cu2O standard sample we measured.[32] A major contribution of surface metallic Cu0 species in the spectrum of the PrC powder can be ruled out due to the absence of the peak at 918.6 eV belonging to metallic

Cu0 and the characteristic peak shape features accompanying the metallic Cu0 peak.[32] Ultimately, O 1s spectra are depicted in Figure 3c to further resolve the nature of the oxide powder. The O 1s peak binding energy of the PrC is found to be neither solely at the position of pure Cu2O, nor solely at the position of CuO. It is assumed to be a sum of the overlap of both Cu+ and Cu2+ species’ lines in a quantitative analysis. The PrC O 1s spectrum reveals a peak binding energy of 530.1 eV and resolves a high binding energy shoulder at ≈531.5 eV. The Cu2O and CuO standard samples show binding energies of 530.4 eV and 529.5 eV, respectively. These values agree well with literature.[33] The standard samples exhibit shoulders at 531.8 eV (in Cu2O) and 531.2 eV (in CuO). These can originate from either hydrated or defective oxygen, hydroxide, water, or organic oxygen.[30,33] The metallic Cu0 standard also shows a peak at ≈531.4 eV, which indicates that this peak most probably originates from organic oxygen and hydroxide. Organic oxygen and hydroxide or water molecules with different contributions on various samples may originate from the vacuum equipment or short transfer of the samples through air. More detailed information about the surface composition is expected from future work with a pure phase Cu4O3 standard sample. The observations made from the XPS measurements prove the presence of predominantly Cu+ as well as Cu2+ species on the surface of the PrC powder. Keeping in mind the results obtained using PXRD and SAED techniques, it can be concluded that the Cu+ species contributions to the XPS results originate from Cu2O and Cu4O3 particles which are present in the powder. On the other hand, Cu4O3 particles in the PrC powder are responsible for Cu2+ species contribution. It should however be mentioned that some Cu2+ contribution can come from a thin and amorphous (as it was not detected by XRD, Figure 1b) native CuO layer.

sections.heading: 2.2. Electrochemical Characterization and CO2RR Activity of a Copper-Based Catalyst Enriched with Paramelaconite
sections.text:
CO2RR catalytic activity and selectivity of PrC powder shown in Figure 1b was experimentally investigated in a flow reactor
equipped with a cathodic carbon-based GDE (10 cm2). Initial chronopotentiometric screening of the catalyst (Figure 4a) was performed employing a flow-by reactor design (Figure 4b and Figure S9, Supporting Information).
The PrC catalyst was screened at different current densities and ethylene was detected as a major CO2RR product. In Figure 4a, the measured change of the negative potential measured at the cathode with increasing current densities is shown. As expected, this change has affected the CO2RR product distribution. This can be seen in Figure 4a, for the case of ethylene, and in Figure S10 (Supporting Information), for all other detected major CO2RR products and HER. Ethylene reached a maximum FEC2H4 of 42.3% at −0.59 V versus RHE, corresponding to experiments performed at jtot = 300 mA cm−2. Other valuable C2+ products, such as ethanol and n-propanol, have also been detected with maximum FE of 14% and 5%, respectively. As ethanol and n-propanol were used in the catalyst synthesis and catalyst ink preparation, we performed an additional control experiment using N2 as feed gas instead of CO2 to confirm that the detected alcohols are indeed CO2RR products (for more detail see the Supporting Information and Figure S11).
To better reference the performance of the PrC, we used the flow-by reactor design to electrochemically characterize a commercially available µ-sized Cu2O powder (Figure S12, Supporting Information). The reference Cu2O powder showed moderate selectivity toward ethylene with a maximum FE of 22% at jtot = 200 mA cm−2 (Figure S12b, Supporting Information). In experiments where the reference Cu2O powder was tested at current densities higher than 300 mA cm−2, hydrogen was the main product, reaching FEH2 of more than 65% at 500 mA cm−2 (Figure S12e, Supporting Information). In contrast, the PrC showed the ability to suppress hydrogen evolution below 28% FE at all tested current densities (Figure S10c, Supporting Information).
As the PrC showed an increased selectivity toward ethylene in the initial electrochemical screening, for our next step we sought to investigate the stability of the PrC under industrially relevant, high current density CO2RR conditions. Total current densities applied in these experiments ranged from

jtot = 100–300 mA cm−2 and were held constant for 2 h. Ethylene Faradaic efficiency for the PrC changed depending on the applied current density. This is to be expected because increasing the current density shifted the negative potentials measured at the cathode to more negative values. A 100 mA cm−2 increase in current density correlated to a ≈165 mV shift in the measured potential at the cathode (Figure 5a). Obtained results at all tested current densities show that there is no time-dependent degradation of the PrC’s selectivity toward ethylene formation after 2 h. With increasing current densities, the FEC2H4 values increased (Figure 5b), achieving the highest value (FEC2H4 of 43% at −0.64 V vs RHE) at the highest investigated current density (jtot = 300 mA cm−2). For the other current densities investigated, jtot = 100 mA cm−2 and jtot = 200 mA cm−2, FEC2H4 reached 24% and 31%, respectively.
Accounting for all detected CO2RR products in the 2 h chronopotentiometric experiments, it can be seen that the product distribution significantly changes with the applied current density (Figure 5c and Figure S13, Supporting Information). After 2 h, the major CO2RR products in the experiment performed at −0.31 V versus RHE (jtot = 100 mA cm−2) were C1 products (FEC1 of 32.3%), predominately formate (FEHCOO− of 23.4%). Increasing the current density led to a decrease in the selectivity toward C1 products, reaching an FEC1 of 26.4% at −0.47 V versus RHE (jtot = 200 mA cm−2) and only an FEC1 of 12.9% at −0.64 V versus RHE (jtot = 300 mA cm−2). Methane formation was found to be suppressed (FECH4 of 0.2%) and only observed at −0.64 V versus RHE. An explanation for methane suppression could be found in the high applied current densities
(>100 mA cm−2) in our experiments which led to higher OH− production rates at the cathode, increasing the local pH at the electrode surface.[34,35] High local pH has been found to inhibit the pH-dependent CO protonation, an accepted mechanism explaining methane formation.[36,37] Additionally, the use of Cs-based electrolytes was also proven to be beneficial for the suppression of C1 products.[38,39] In contrast to C1 products, the C2+ product formation was intensified as current density was increased. Detected C2+ products were ethylene, acetate, ethanol and n-propanol (Figure S14, Supporting Information). In all experiments, the major C2+ product was found to be ethylene. The lowest selectivity toward C2+ products was FEC1 of 30% at −0.31 V versus RHE (jtot = 100 mA cm−2), followed by FE2+ of 44.6% at −0.47 V versus RHE (jtot = 200 mA cm−2). At −0.64 V versus RHE, Faradaic efficiency for C2+ products reached its peak value of FEC2+ of 61.7%, with a corresponding partial current density of jC2+ = 185 mA cm
−2, and a high C2+/C1 product ratio of 4.8. Besides ethylene, a noticeable Faradaic efficiency value was measured for ethanol (FEEtOH of 13.4%) at −0.64 V versus RHE. It was observed that an increase in selectivity toward ethylene was always followed by an increase ethanol formation, which can be accredited to common C1 intermediates in their reaction pathways.[3,40,41] The hydrogen evolution reaction was below FEH2 = 30% at all tested current densities. SEM images, showing the morphology of the catalyst before and after the experiments, revealed that the surface of both Cu4O3 and Cu2O particles underwent a roughening process (Figure 5e,d). Besides surface roughening, no other significant morphological degradation of the particles was observed after 2 h.

To test the limits of the PrC, an additional long-term chronopotentiometric experiment (Figure S14, Supporting Information) was performed. Over the course of 24 h the PrC showed stable FE for ethylene, reaching a maximum of FEC2H4 of 35% under a constant current density of jtot = 200 mA cm−2 (Figure 5f). For comparison, dendritic copper structures which are currently considered as state-of-the-art catalysts for CO2 reduction (ref. [4,7]), typically show degradation in their catalytic performance after 1 h at current densities higher than 150 mA cm−2. This can be partially attributed to structural changes that occur during electrolysis. The fine nanodendritic structures coarsen over time due to the local dissolution/redeposition processes of copper. Degradation of the fine structures ultimately leads to the loss of high index facets containing low coordinated sites which are believed to be responsible for ethylene formation.[42] The exceptional long-term stability of PrC on a traditional carbon-based GDE under industrially relevant, high-current density conditions is compared with other recently reported state-of-the-art copper-based catalysts (Table S2, Supporting Information). Unlike the dendrites, micrometer-sized spherical paramelaconite particles are more structurally robust and not as prone to structural degradation in the first hours of the electrolysis (Figure 5e,d). However, after 24 h a decrease in FEC2H4 was observed, followed by an increased rate of H2 formation. One of the reasons for such performance degradation can be found in the fact that a noticeable amount of permeate was observed coming through the GDE into the CO2 gas chamber after 24 h of operation. Flooding of GDEs is a known problem which ultimately leads to stability issues when performing CO2 electroreduction in flow reactors. Flooding of commercially available gas diffusion layers happens due to their loss of hydrophobicity when exposed to cathodic operation conditions needed for CO2 electroreduction.[43] As a result of flooding, the necessary three phase boundary which is needed for reducing CO2 is lost because of blocked CO2 diffusion pathways which led to the catalyst’s surface. SEM investigation of the catalyst particles performed after the particles were exposed to operational conditions for more than 24 h showed that the roughening process of the surface of the particles continued over time. This eventually led to the formation of micrometersized dendritic structures on top of the Cu4O3 and the Cu2O particles (Figure S15, Supporting Information). By blocking the initial active sites and introducing new ones with different exposed crystal facets, the in situ formed dendritic structures influence the CO2RR product distribution. Besides flooding, this can also be one of the reasons for the observed decrease in FEC2H4 and the increased rate of CH4 and H2 formation. Finally, deactivation of the catalytic sites due to electrodeposition of trace metal impurities coming from the electrolyte has been identified as one of the problems inhibiting long-term stable electrolysis.[10,44] To investigate this possibility, we have characterized our cathode’s surface after the 24 h electrolysis using XPS. The XPS data (Figure S16, Supporting Information) revealed the contamination of the electrode’s surface with trace impurities of Zn, coming from the electrolyte. Together with the previously mentioned issues, the poisoning of the active surface additionally contributes to the observed deactivation after 24 h.

sections.heading: 2.3. Stability of the PrC’s Surface Oxide Species during CO2RR
sections.text:
The performance of a catalyst is directly related to the state of its surface during operation. Thus, it is critical to understand what surface species are present. The role of copper oxidation state and subsurface oxygen in hydrocarbon formation during CO2RR has been a topic of a wide debate.[20] However, based on the most recent theoretical[20,21] and experimental work,[18,19,45] it now seems clear that surface copper oxides are unstable under CO2RR conditions and that existence of any near-surface residual oxides, which would actually have an effect on the CO2RR, is highly improbable. By employing CV studies and postelectrolysis, ex situ XPS measurements of PrC samples, we were also able to observe the reduction of surface oxide species after exposure to negative potentials at the cathode, suggesting that Cu0 is the active phase during electrolysis. As established previously, the pristine PrC powder contains Cu+ and Cu2+ surface species. To investigate the stability of the mentioned oxides during operating conditions, we exposed the catalyst to a constant potential of −0.7 V versus RHE for 2 h (Figure S17, Supporting Information) and characterized the surface chemistry of the sample after electrolysis using ex situ XPS. Before starting the chronoamperometric measurement, cyclic voltammetry (CV) was performed. Data obtained from the CV curves (Figure S18, Supporting Information) provides evidence that two surface reduction events took place, corresponding to the reduction of Cu+ and Cu2+ surface species. The second CV cycle did not show any reduction events, suggesting that the surface did not re-oxidize across the examined potential range. Two additional CVs were measured, one was measured 15 min into the experiment and the other was measured just before stopping the experiment. Both CVs did not exhibit any reduction events, indicating a reduced metallic nature of the catalyst’s surface during operation. After 2 h, the experiment was stopped and postelectrolysis, ex situ XPS was employed to provide further evidence concerning the reduction events which were observed during electrolysis. Before and after electrolysis XPS spectra (Figure S18, Supporting Information) provide some evidence that a reduction of surface oxide species took place (appearance of a peak in the Cu L3M4,5M4,5 region which is characteristic for metallic copper). Unfortunately, due to the ex situ nature of the XPS measurements, we could not prevent the spontaneous reoxidation of the catalyst’s surface after potential cut-off. This is the reason why signals corresponding to Cu2O were still observed in the XPS spectra of the sample which was exposed to a negative potential at the cathode. In their work Yeo et al. used in-situ Raman spectroscopy to demonstrate that rapid re-oxidation of copper surfaces happens already 60 s after potential cut-off.[23] In a different publication, Lum et al. came to similar conclusions.[18] Besides the surface sensitive XPS technique, we additionally employed bulk sensitive characterization methods, such as PXRD (Figure S19, Supporting Information) and TEM SAED (Figure S20, Supporting Information), to characterize the PrC after electrolysis. Both techniques gave evidence of Cu4O3 presence in the bulk of the powder. Considering the information obtained from the CV and XPS measurements which showed the reduction of surface oxide species, we can presume that the Cu4O3 detected via PXRD and TEM SAED originates only from

the bulk of the micrometer-sized paramelaconite particles. Unlike Cu2O and CuO, paramelaconite will not be reformed by re-oxidation after exposure to air at ambient conditions or under open circuit potential (OCP) conditions. This makes paramelaconite-based catalysts suitable for a wide range of postelectrolysis, ex situ characterization techniques. Combining the information obtained from surface- and bulk-sensitivity investigations, we propose that the paramelaconite acts as a precatalyst, forming both the surface-active Cu0 phase and the residual bulk oxide support for the surface active sites at the micrometer-sized, spherical Cu4O3 particles. In a recent work, where a copper-oxide-based catalyst was used for CO2 reduction, it was suggested that a suitable oxide sublayer is beneficial for improving the selectivity toward hydrocarbon products.[46] The synergetic catalytic effect of an oxide support and its active phase are also recognized outside of the CO2 electroreduction field, where some of the most known examples are the Cu/ ZrO2 and Cu/ZrO2/Al2O3 catalysts for CO2 hydrogenation to methanol.[47–49] A complete understanding of the observed stability of the residual bulk Cu4O3 phase under CO2RR conditions is not yet clear and further investigations on a phase pure material are needed. However, a possible explanation could be that extremely alkaline conditions at the cathode’s surface (local pH ≈ 14) cause the shifting of the overpotential for Cu4O3 reduction toward more negative values. This would potentially help stabilize the residual bulk Cu4O3 which then acts as a support oxide layer for the surface-active Cu0 phase. As for the Cu2O particles present in the PrC powder, from previous work, it clear that the Cu+ species also undergo a reduction and form a surface-active Cu0 phase.[18–21,45]
From the presented results it can be seen that the synthesized PrC catalyst enables a stable CO2RR process at low overpotentials (−0.64 V vs RHE) with high selectivity for C2+ products (FEC2+ of 61.7%). However, it is still difficult to conclude what effect, precisely, the paramelaconite phase has on the CO2RR. This difficulty arises from the fact that there are Cu2O particles present in the PrC powder, which makes it problematic to distinguish between the intrinsic contributions of Cu2O and Cu4O3 on the CO2RR. However, results obtained from a recent DFT study, which calculated adsorption of a CO molecule on a Cu4O3(202) basal plane, suggested that the intrinsic properties of a Cu4O3 mixed-valence surface could contribute to an increased hydrocarbon formation.[50] The study reported that when a CO molecule is adsorbed on to a Cu4O3 surface, it reacts with the surface oxygen to form CO2. The CO2 molecule is then desorbed, leaving an oxygen vacancy at the surface. Further calculations revealed that such a Cu4O3 surface, rich in oxygen vacancies, has the lowest energy barrier for CC bond formation, compared to Cu2O and CuO surfaces. Besides lowering the energy barrier for CC bond formation, the mixedvalence Cu4O3 surface possesses the ability to electrostatically stabilize the highly polar (OC)δ+(CO)δ-dimer that is proposed as an important intermediate in the formation of many C2+ products.[51] To date, there have been no experimental studies which investigated the catalytic activity of the paramelaconite phase for CO2RR. Nonetheless, certain previous works have claimed that having a copper-oxide-based catalyst with a mixed-valence surface species is beneficial for reducing CO2 to hydrocarbons. For example, Daiyan et al. have correlated the increased FE for
ethanol to the presence of Cu+/Cu2+ interfaces at the surface of a 3D, heterostructured copper electrode.[46] In another study, performed by Xiao et al., it was found that mixed-valence surface is beneficial for boosting the efficiency and selectivity of CO2RR. The authors claimed that the synergy between Cu+ and Cu0 surface species led to improved kinetics and thermodynamics of both CO2 activation and CO dimerization.[28]

sections.heading: 3. Conclusion
sections.text: In summary, we have investigated a copper-based catalyst enriched with Cu4O3 and demonstrated that this catalyst performs stably under industrially relevant current densities, forming ethylene as the main product. Using an up-scaled and modified solvothermal synthesis route, we were able to successfully synthesize a PrC powder which showed high selectivity toward ethylene (FEC2H4 of 43%) and high catalytic activity (jtot = 300 mA cm−2), at a low applied potential at the cathode of only −0.64 V versus RHE. Based on the postelectrolysis characterization of the catalyst, using both surface- and bulk-sensitive techniques, we suggest that the Cu4O3 particles present in the PrC powder act as a precatalyst. During operation, the surfaceactive phase is formed through the reduction of copper-oxide species present at the surface. In the bulk, however, presence of paramelaconite phase could still be detected suggesting that the residual bulk oxide could act as a support for the Cu0 surfaceactive sites at the micrometer-sized, spherical Cu4O3 particles. In addition, to its high catalytic activity, selectivity toward C2+ products and ability to operate at low overpotentials, we demonstrated that the PrC is also stable during a 24 h CO2RR at 200 mA cm−2. As discussed previously, due to the presence of Cu2O particles in the PrC powder, it was difficult to investigate how the intrinsic properties of Cu4O3 affected the CO2RR. To shed more light on this matter, we are currently working on developing a phase pure Cu4O3 powder. This will allow us to fully characterize (experimentally and theoretically) the paramelaconite phase as a catalyst for CO2RR, more clearly understand the reduction mechanism of CO2 on the paramelaconite’s mixed-valence surface, and compare it to the current state-ofthe-art copper-based catalysts.

sections.heading: 4. Experimental Section
sections.text:
Catalyst Synthesis: The catalyst powders containing paramelaconite were prepared by dissolving Cu(NO3)2·3H2O (50 × 10−3 m) in an ethanol-DMF solvent mixture with the addition of formic acid and dimethylamine (10–40 × 10−3 m) (further details in the Supporting Information). The reaction mixture was held inside an autoclave for 20–72 h under 130 °C. After the desired reaction time, the reaction mixture was cooled down to room temperature using an ice bath, the supernatant was removed, and the remaining precipitated solid product was collected by centrifugation. Obtained powders were then washed with ethanol and deionized water five times, dried under vacuum and stored inside an inert glove-box atmosphere.
Material Characterization: Secondary electron imaging (SE) in the SEM (ZEISS Crossbeam 540, FEG) was used to characterize catalyst and GDE morphology before and after CO2RR electrolysis experiments. Powder X-ray diffraction data were obtained using a Bruker D2 PHASER diffractometer, using Cu K radiation, at a scan rate of 0.02° s−1. Once

© 2019 WILEY-VCH Verlag GmbH & Co. KGaA, Weinheim1901228 (9 of 10)
the experiments were completed, special care was taken to minimize the air exposure of the catalyst. After the electrolysis experiment was ended, GDEs were immediately taken out of the flow cell, rinsed with copious amounts of MilliQ water, dried under an Ar gas stream and stored inside an inert glovebox atmosphere. Inside the glovebox, GDE samples was prepared for XRD measurement using a special airtight specimen holder which eliminated prolonged air exposure of the sample during the XRD measurement. TEM SAED measurements were performed using a 200 kV JEOL JEM-2200FS transmission electron microscope. The TEM samples were prepared utilizing the standard in-situ lift of procedure with an FEI STRATA dual-beam focused ion beam (FIB)-SEM. Before extracting the TEM sample, protective layers of platinum were deposited using the electron and ion beams. XPS was performed on a commercially available Quantera II instrument (Physical Electronics Inc., Chanhassen, MN, USA). Monochromated Al Kα X-rays (1486.6 eV) from a source operating at 15 kV and 50 W were focused on spots of ≈200 × 200 µm2 on the samples. All powder samples were mounted by the use of insulating double-sided adhesive tape and the outmost layer of powder was knocked off to make a pristine surface accessible for the measurement. Emitted photoelectrons were detected at analyzer pass energies of 280 eV (for survey), 140 eV (for C 1s) and 69 eV (for Cu 2p, Cu LMM, O 1s). The CasaXPS software (Casa Software Ltd.) was applied to analyze the experimentally obtained spectra. The binding energy scale was referenced to the C 1s core level at 284.8 eV from which an estimated error of 0.2 eV arises. The Cu2O (purity ≥99.99%) and CuO (purity 99.999%) standard samples were obtained from Sigma-Aldrich (Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany), prepared in a glove box and transferred to the XPS vacuum chamber while minimizing the exposure to air. For metallic Cu0, the sputter cleaned standard sample provided by the manufacturer of the instrument was used.
GDE Preparation: A gas diffusion layer (GDL) (Freudenberg H23C2) which contains a microporous carbon black layer and a fiber-based PTFE-bounded back bone was used as catalyst support. Catalyst ink was prepared by dispersing the catalyst powder (90 mg) in 1-propanol (3 mL). Additionally, Sustainion XA-9 ionomer (Dioxide Materials) (25 µL) was added to the catalyst ink. The mixture was sonicated for 20 min. The GDE was then prepared by air-brushing the prepared catalyst ink on top of the GDL. After air-brushing, the GDE was left to dry overnight at room temperature. The GDL was weighted before and after catalyst deposition to determine the catalyst loading. The catalyst loading was determined to be 1.5 mg cm−2 (± 0.2). During spray coating, ≈50 wt% of catalyst was lost. Both the GDEs containing PrC and the reference Cu2O powder were prepared following the same procedure as described above.
Electrochemical Characterization and Measurements: The shortterm (2 h) chronopotentiometric electrochemical investigations were carried out in a stacked three compartment flow cell purchased from ElectroCell (Micro Flow Cell). The cathode and anode compartments which contained the catholyte and anolyte were separated by a cation exchange membrane (Nafion 117). The third compartment (CO2 gas chamber) was located behind the cathode chamber and separated from the catholyte with a GDE (10 cm2) which served as a cathode (Supporting Figure 5). Electrolytes were pumped in two separate cycles through the cell. In the short-term (2 h) 0.5 m Cs2SO4 was used as catholyte and 2.5 m KOH was used as anolyte. All electrolyte solutions were prepared with ultrapure water (18.2 MΩ cm, MilliQ Millipore system). Electrolyte flow was controlled using a peristaltic pump (Ismatec ECOLINE VC-MS/CA8-6) which kept the flow constant at 40 mL min−1. CO2 gas (Air Liquide, 99.995%) was used without further purification. It was continuously supplied to the flow cell at atmospheric pressure, at different constant flow rates: 45 mL min−1 for 100 mA cm−2 applied, 90 mL min−1 for 200 mA cm−2 applied, and 135 mL min−1 for 300 mA cm−2 applied. The gas flow was controlled with a mass flow controller (Bronkhorst). The cell was fitted with an Ag/AgCl (3 m KCl) reference electrode. The pH value of the catholyte was monitored throughout the experiment using a pH electrode (Metrohm). For chronoamperometric measurements the cathode was connected as working electrode. As anode, a Ti sheet coated with
Ir-MMO (iridium-mixed metal oxide) obtained from ElectroCell was used in all experiments. For the 24 h electrolysis experiment, a slightly different flow cell configuration was used (Figure S8, Supporting Information). The catholyte and anolyte were no longer separated. As electrolyte, a mixture of 0.5 m CsHCO3 and 0.1 m Cs2SO4 was used as both catholyte and anolyte. After every cycle the electrolyte was mixed once again enabling the continuous balancing of cations, anions, pH and water in the system throughout the experiment. The Nafion membrane was replaced with a ZrO2 diaphragm. This change was introduced to overcome the following problem. In the short-term (2 h) cell configuration, with time, the concentration of potassium ions (KOH) in the anolyte was decreasing proportional to the charge flow. The decrease in concentration was happening due to the fact that the potassium ions were migrating through the Nafion membrane into the catholyte. This process would go on until only water would be left as anolyte, hindering the possibility of a long-term running system. Additionally, increasing concentrations of potassium ions inside the catholyte would cause precipitation of potassium salt crystals on the GDE’s surface, inhibiting its performance. Because the electrolyte was constantly mixed and recirculated through the cathode and anode chamber, analysis of the liquid products was not possible. The liquid products obtained at the cathode reactions would get oxidized on the anode. All electrochemical measurements were conducted on a Metrohm Autolab PGSTAT302N potentiostate-galvanostate. All measurements were performed without iR-drop compensation. The obtained Ag/AgCl electrode potentials were converted to the RHE scale using the following equation: ERHE = EAg/AgCl + 0.21V + 0.0591 pH.
CO2RR Product Analysis: For all experiments, except the long-term 24 h chronopotentiometric electrolysis, gas samples were taken every 15 min using gas sample bags and analyzed by a Thermo Scientific Trace 1310 gas chromatograph (GC) equipped with two thermal conductivity detector (TCD) channels. In the case of the long-term chronopotentiometric electrolysis the output gas from the flow reactor was directly routed to the GC. The hydrocarbons were separated with a micropacked GC column (Shincarbon, Restek, Bellefonte, PA, USA) with He as carrier. Hydrogen values were measured on a packed 5 Å mol-sieve column (Restek, Bellefonte, PA, USA) using Ar as carrier. Liquid products were analyzed using nuclear magnetic resonance. 1H NMR spectra where recorded on a 400 MHz Bruker Avance 400 spectrometer equipped with an auto tune BBO, 5 mm, Ag-31P probe head, a pulsed field gradient unit and gradient shimming unit. NMR samples were prepared by the following method. 250 µL of D2O and 50 µL of an internal standard stock solution containing 0.06 m dimethyl sulfone in water were added to 300 µL electrolyte. The electrolyte is diluted 1:2 and the final sample contains 5 × 10−3 m internal standard. FEs of the liquid and gas products were obtained using Equation (1)
